newsitem.title: USA: Miami meets budget deadline but still has deficits.
newsitem.headline: Miami meets budget deadline but still has deficits.

text.p: Miami met a state deadline to draft a five-year budget by Tuesday but the proposal still has annual deficits of $16 million to $42 million in the last three years, city officials said.

The budget was to be submitted Tuesday to the state oversight board that is guiding Miami's fiscal recovery. A spokesman for the board chairman, Lt. Gov. Buddy MacKay, said it was unclear whether the deficits for 1999-2001 would prompt rejection of the plan.
"That will be up to the board to decide whether in fact the city has met the terms," said MacKay's press spokesman, Jim McClellan.
MacKay has not seen the budget but "was very pleased they met the deadline," McClellan said. "He thought that showed they are serious about getting out of this mess."

The board rejected the city's request last week to extend the deadline. The board staff will review the plan Friday with city officials and seek comment from municipal bond rating agencies, McClellan said. The board will then review it at a public meeting Monday.

Miami's City commission unanimously approved the final piece of the budget, a $24 million fire service tax, Monday night. It eliminates Miami's annual garbage collection fee of $166 and replaces it with the fire district fee that starts at $166 for single-family homes and rises according to property type and size.
Unlike the garbage fee, the fire-rescue fee is levied on tax-exempt property owned by the Dade County government, the county school board and non-profit institutions.
The new fee will raise $24 million annunally, or about $13 million above the cost of services. The surplus will go into the city's general fund, offsetting other fixed costs.

State law requires cities to balance their budgets. After several Miami officials resigned in a corruption scandal last fall, the city discovered a $68 million deficit in its $275 million budget for the year that began Oct 1, 1996.
Gov. Lawton Chiles appointed the financial oversight board to ride herd on Miami's finances and could take control of the city if it fails to fix its problems.

Miami has already balanced the 1997 budget with employee concessions, service cuts and one-time revenues such as proceeds from land sales. The proposed 1998 budget is also balanced, but the remaining years in the five-year plan have deficits that start at $16 million in 1999 and rise to $42 million in 2001, Assistant City Manager Bob Nachlinger said.
The city is still looking for new revenues and cost cutting measures for those years, he said.
"Probablyfore that budget is to commence, we'll be working to make sure it's balanced," Nachlinger said.
